items.summary: A November 21, 2026 comparison of seven personal AI agents ranked them by memory transparency, security isolation and cost. The category began with OpenClaw (originally Clawdbot) as a weekend project launched November 2025 before Google, OpenAI, Meta and Perplexity shipped their own versions within about twelve months; products split into self-hosted options running on user hardware versus managed agents bundled with vendor subscriptions. Hermes Agent scored highest for developers because it stores editable Markdown memory files (MEMORY.md, USER.md) in SQLite-backed session history and defaults fail-closed by denying unanswered approval prompts after 300 seconds, though its docs admit the denylist does not sandbox a compromised agent and OS-level isolation is the only load-bearing boundary. OpenClaw offered channel breadth across 26 platforms but was flagged as risky because it grants full host access by default; an incident record cited CVE-2026-25253 for one-click remote code execution via WebSocket origin bypass, plus a Koi Security audit of 2,857 ClawHub skills finding 341 malicious entries (later counted at 1,184), prompting mandatory VirusTotal scanning and daily re-scans. Among managed agents, Meta Muse published the most detailed isolation design with a Sentinel agent gating network access on a dedicated VM, while Gemini Spark relied on Google account data as memory without an editable store; OpenAI dots drew on saved notes plus read-only research between requests; Perplexity Personal Computer merged cloud and local Mac work but lacked a documented memory model. All seven agents are free software or offer free tiers with subscription pricing (Spark $99.99 AI Ultra, later folded into the $20 US AI Pro plan), while self-hosted options incur only token spend plus hosting costs that can exceed chat usage due to always-on background work like heartbeat checks and scheduled jobs.
items.title: Personal AI Agents Compared on Memory, Security and Cost in 2026

items.summary: A letter published in a forum titled 'Afford the dead some dignity' by Edwin Tan Tiat Heng describes his experience identifying his late wife's body after her death was classified as a coroner's case at Singapore General Hospital. Because the cause of death had to be determined via post-mortem before release and issuance of a death certificate, the family expected a longer wait but were instead shown how the remains were displayed: wrapped in a translucent plastic sheet on a metal trolley with no covering or proper repose. The author found this treatment distressing, noting that funeral directors and embalmers—who he credited for their efforts—described it as routine. He argued that compassion toward living people should extend to the dead, who cannot protest, and called for greater respect and dignity in handling remains. The account is a single personal observation of one incident at Block 9's mortuary; no hospital policy or broader data are presented, so its findings reflect only this individual's experience rather than established practice.
items.title: Singapore General Hospital reader criticizes mortuary handling of a deceased relative's body

items.summary: In a forum post titled 'Are we missing important indicators of heart disease risk?', contributor Koh Chin Chye raises questions about whether conventional LDL cholesterol testing alone adequately captures cardiovascular risk. The piece notes that while LDL is the primary marker discussed in routine screenings, ApoB—which measures the number of potentially harmful cholesterol-carrying particles rather than just the amount of cholesterol they carry—and Lp(a)—a largely genetically determined inherited factor—may offer a more complete picture. Koh frames these markers as relevant to preventive healthcare specifically within Singapore and poses several questions: whether ApoB and Lp(a) tests are routinely accessible through local GPs, polyclinics, and hospitals; whether individuals with elevated LDL or family history should pursue further assessment; whether one-time adult testing is warranted given Lp(a)'s inherited nature; and whether healthcare professionals incorporate these markers into risk assessments. The post concludes by suggesting that as Singapore emphasizes preventive care, cardiovascular evaluation may benefit from looking beyond cholesterol numbers alone. No evidence in the text supports claims about test availability or current clinical practice; it presents only a single contributor's perspective and open questions rather than established findings.
items.title: Singaporean Contributor Questions Whether ApoB and Lp(a) Testing Should Be Integrated Into Routine Cardiovascular Risk Assessment

items.summary: Google has launched Tool Retrieval, a preview feature of the Gemini API's Interactions API that defers tool parameter schemas until the model requests them. The motivation is token cost: Google states that a few dozen function declarations can consume tens of thousands of tokens per request when loaded statically. With defer_loading enabled (adding {"type": "tool_search"} to the tools array and setting defer_loading: true on each function), models see only tool names and short descriptions, receiving full schemas only after requesting them via a three-step response—tool_search_call by name, an API-supplied tool_search_result with the schema, and a model-emitted function_call that the app executes. Google advises static loading for libraries under 20 stable tools rather than deferring. The feature runs server-side (default) or client-side; in server mode search, load, and call resolve within one API request with no index to host, while client mode uses execution: "client" and costs one extra round trip per search. Only one tool_search entry is allowed per request, the two modes cannot be combined, and deferred MCP tools still execute remotely through Gemini's MCP support. There is no separate fee; tokens bill at standard input/cached/output rates, with each server-side search adding a model call over full context (counted in total_tool_use_tokens) and loaded schemas billed as input for the rest of the conversation—though Google notes static loading may be cheaper for small libraries or per-turn searches. Compared to Anthropic's self-reported 85% savings and OpenAI's 47%, Google published no comparable figures, so these numbers are not directly comparable.
items.title: Google Launches Tool Retrieval (Deferred Schema Loading) in the Gemini API

items.summary: As parliament enters its final four days before a December recess in 2026, the Australian government faces uncertainty over which reforms will pass amid last-minute negotiations. Several key policies remain stalled in the Senate—the domestic gas reserve, changes to trusts and capital gains tax, the digital duty of care bill, and private health insurance—with Labor sources confident some may advance as Anthony Albanese returns from Manila and Shenzhen to intensify deal-making. However, Greens and Coalition negotiators have signaled reluctance to grant quick wins; while a gas agreement appears closer after Labor promised a Western Australia carveout that both sides view as pressure tactics rather than genuine compromise on fossil fuels, the digital duty of care bill may find more traction since it only recommends one key amendment allowing citizens legal action against big tech. On AI policy, the joint select committee's report expected Monday could reveal whether bipartisan consensus holds or fractures over contentious issues like datacentres and copyright compensation for creatives whose work is used by AI companies—a proposal that drew criticism from musicians supporting Not AI's To Take campaign while senior Labor figures increasingly reject the status quo despite rightsholder groups disputing the need for change. Foreign affairs minister Penny Wong will separately frame AI as a national security matter, urging global cooperation over speed-driven development.
items.title: Final Days of 2026 Parliament: AI Report, Gas Deal, and Copyright Tensions

items.summary: In an opinion piece titled 'As the real world falls apart, Grand Theft Auto looks more and more appealing,' writer Dave Schilling argues that recent disruptions to technology infrastructure have made video games like Grand Theft Auto VI (recently released) seem increasingly attractive. The author notes that millions of people turned away from their responsibilities to play GTA VI despite his own lack of interest in the game. He describes a wave of tech outages over the past week—including grounded planes, broken email systems, and unstable bank accounts—attributed by experts to software bugs, faulty patches, and outdated equipment, though some observers have blamed hackers or government manipulation. Schilling observes that AI companies like Anthropic are expanding their integration into daily life while ordinary users bear the cost of inaccessible services; he suggests the main beneficiaries beyond tech firms may be airport bar owners who profit when systems fail. The writer draws parallels between real-life frustrations and video game mechanics, comparing health insurance claims to boss fights in Sonic the Hedgehog and imagining himself as a powerless NPC character subject to algorithmic control. He concludes that these technological failures reinforce people's dependence on their devices—citing Microsoft Outlook crashes and Chase bank outages as reminders of what users take for granted—and argues that this dependency ultimately drives individuals further into digital entertainment like GTA VI, where they retain agency unavailable in real life before the holiday season.
items.title: Opinion: Tech Outages Make Grand Theft Auto VI More Appealing

items.summary: Starting Tuesday, Wells Fargo is updating its agreement with millions of customers to state that use of any third-party AI agent is at the user's own risk. This move reflects a broader push by US banks against autonomous shopping agents: in late October, JPMorgan Chase changed terms to ban third-party agents logging in with customer credentials, Bank of America warned users not to share login information with agents, and Citibank and PNC also updated their terms to include agent warnings. The concern centers on the automation that these always-on agents provide—users authorize goals rather than every individual click, so a bot can make costly errors such as posting bank details publicly or purchasing an unintended quantity of goods; Luca Cian's hypothetical example is a customer whose agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from a supermarket. Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst focusing on ecommerce and consumer behavior, characterizes banks as fundamentally risk-averse and taking proactive measures to cover potential issues if agentic tools persist rather than fade away. Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging technology, notes that while some consumers may feel it is unfair to be held accountable for their agent's mistakes, she does not expect these policy changes to deter early adopters already using the tools daily. Luca Cian adds that many users are aware of the risks and limit control to certain tasks such as household supplies rather than dynamic big-ticket purchases requiring discretion. American Express has separately announced that some agentic errors may become eligible for reimbursement through its card provider if a customer cannot recover funds from the original retailer. The banks' warnings coexist with their investment in first-party tools: Wells Fargo's generative AI tool was interacted with over one billion times, Bank of America revamped its EricaAssist agent this year, and Citigroup launched an internal development platform centered on agents. Sucharita Kodali remains skeptical that the precautions are necessary, arguing that buying directly from retailers like Amazon or Walmart is not difficult in most transactions and does not require an agent.
items.title: Wells Fargo and Other Banks Warn Customers of Risk From Third-Party AI Agents

items.summary: In an interview on Rapid Response, hosted by Robert Safian of the Masters of Scale team, CrowdStrike founder and CEO George Kurtz addressed a week-long series of major system outages—including Microsoft systems, air traffic control, Chase, United Airlines, and Apple—and attributed them to AI-driven acceleration in vulnerability discovery rather than coincidence. Kurtz argued that Mythos, released nine months prior, triggered an industry-wide effort to identify vulnerabilities and produce patches; the sector has now reached a limit on patch rollout speed, resulting in what he called 'Black October' followed by 'Darker November.' He cited Java as likely worse than PHP due to existing working exploits. According to Kurtz, organizations are being forced into a new norm of choosing between accepting a breach from slow patching or risking system breakage during rushed deployments—a tradeoff worsened by legacy systems and midstream operations that complicate fixes. The interview excerpt ends before covering his discussion of CrowdStrike's AI Kill Switch product and his assertion that slowing frontier labs would not reduce attacker capability, so those claims are not presented here as established findings.
items.title: CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz: Organizations Face 'Breach or Break' Dilemma Amid AI-Accelerated Vulnerabilities

items.summary:
The Camp Fire of 2018, which killed 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 structures near Paradise, California after a live wire from Pacific Gas and Electric Co.'s transmission tower ignited brush, settled for $13.5 billion—among the largest civil settlements for an environmental disaster in U.S. history—and drove PG&E into bankruptcy. Since 2017, more than $18 billion has been awarded or agreed to in civil wildfire settlements across California, Hawaiʻi, Colorado, and Oregon, with utilities such as PG&E, PacifiCorp, Xcel Energy, and Southern California Edison bearing the largest share of claims.

The surge is attributed partly to worsening fire conditions: after a mild winter that produced one of the lightest snowpacks in recent history, more than 9 million acres burned across the U.S. as of October—about 1.5 times the past-decade average for the year to date, per the National Interagency Fire Center. Stanford climate scientist Chris Field noted that while California has not seen a large increase in fire numbers, warming landscapes and development have raised the probability that small fires grow into catastrophic ones.

Litigation concentrates on ignition liability under strict standards: California's inverse condemnation allows utilities to be held liable even without negligence, whereas jury verdicts elsewhere—such as more than $1 billion against PacifiCorp over Oregon's 2020 Labor Day fires (later reversed by the Oregon Court of Appeals)—are less common. Claims are typically handled as mass torts with contingency fees between 30% and 40%, though Hawaiʻi caps reasonable attorney fees at 25%. The 2023 Maui wildfires settlement totaled $4 billion, including $1.99 billion from Hawaiian Electric Industries and its subsidiary and $800 million from the state of Hawaiʻi; a judge capped attorneys' fees at $222 million after plaintiffs had hoped for about $1 billion.

The industry has expanded rapidly: Singleton Schreiber's San Diego firm now employs roughly 200 staff on wildfire cases, having represented over 30,000 victims and recovered $3 billion. California firms increasingly litigate claims in other states, with Nature Conservancy fire director Marek Smith describing the effect as exponential since last year's Southern California and Los Angeles wildfires.

The article notes several caveats: litigation finance from hedge funds such as Jefferies Financial Group Inc. and Oppenheimer Holdings Inc. carries annualized interest above 20%, a practice some lawyers oppose; Western states, including California, are considering legislation to protect utilities; and legal analysts dispute whether holding one entity responsible is fair given collective contributors like fossil fuel companies and federal fire-suppression policies.

No chart was provided or clearly warranted by the text.
items.title: Wildfire Litigation Has Become a Multibillion-Dollar Industry in the U.S.

items.summary:
Briggs & Stratton introduced a new 16 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) backup battery that expands the capacity of its EG4-branded, all-American-made SimpliPHI storage line. The company partnered with Texas-based EG4 last year on stackable batteries for home energy projects; those earlier units were limited in size and capability. This new pack lets a single system scale up to 512 kWh when stacked. Briggs & Stratton states that the average US home uses about 865 kWh per month, so it frames the 512 kWh capacity as theoretically providing nearly 18 days of power after an outage or weekend-level service for a whole block. Sequoya Cross, vice president of energy storage at Briggs & Stratton, described the launch as "a significant shift in our battery strategy," citing combined resources to offer installers a competitively priced, high-quality unit.

The SimpliPHI 16 includes an onboard battery management system and built-in Wi-Fi gateway for setup streamlining, automatic inverter sensing with closed-loop communication across Sol-Ark, Solis, EG4, Growatt, Megarevo, Victron, and other inverters, an IP65-rated enclosure allowing indoor or outdoor ground- or wall-mounted installation without a separate cabinet, and an integrated circuit breaker for servicing isolation. The battery is rated at 8,000 cycles at 90% depth of discharge, with charge and discharge rates of 0.5C and end-of-life capacity of 70%. Briggs & Stratton backs the packs with a 12-year parts warranty covering labor and travel plus US-based tech support.

The SimpliPHI 16 is available for pre-order now; pricing was not disclosed in the original press release, which limits direct cost comparisons. The article also contains promotional content directing readers to EnergySage for solar installer quotes, separate from the product announcement.
items.title: Briggs & Stratton launches 16 kWh SimpliPHI lithium battery, extending its stackable system up to 512 kWh

items.summary:
On an early-morning Sunday in September 2025, Sea Shepherd Conservation Society crew aboard the MV Sharkwater intercepted seven men camping on Isla Desterrada inside Alacranes (Scorpion) Reef National Park—about 70 miles off northern Yucatán and home to the Gulf of Mexico's largest coral reef. The park spans more than 1,300 square miles; its five vegetated islands permit visitors only at one site, while fishing requires special permits that were absent from a daily authorized-vessel list maintained by Mexico's National Commission of Natural Protected Areas. Drone imagery had identified the boat as unlisted before dawn, prompting Sea Shepherd and accompanying Mexican officials to board on shore—where authorities can legally detain people—to issue a citation carrying fines up to about $50,000 (1 million pesos). The crew reported that waters grew noticeably calmer after roughly 18 patrols over the prior year and a half, during which they helped intercept nearly 50 vessels for permit violations or illegal fishing. Sea Shepherd began this joint campaign in March 2025 at the request of Tomás Camarena, director of Alacranes Reef National Park; earlier efforts were hampered by insufficient boats and fuel for the roughly seven-hour voyage from Progreso to reach the reef.

The article frames these patrols within broader context: Mexico joined nearly 200 countries in adopting the Kunming-Montreal Biodiversity Framework, committing to protect 30% of marine areas by 2030 ("30×30"); roughly a quarter of globally designated protected ocean areas lack adequate funding and enforcement; and about 25% of Mexico's marine areas are legally protected. Coral reefs reportedly host at least 25% of all marine life, including around 4,000 fish species, but global warming is driving approximately 96% of the world's shallow reefs toward collapse—underscoring scientists' view that well-managed protected areas help corals resist heat stress by reducing local pressures like overfishing.

A key limitation to enforcement effectiveness was stated: patrols run only for a week or two at a time, leaving the reef vulnerable when absent; Sea Shepherd aims for 24/7 coverage in both Scorpion Reef and Bajos del Norte National Park within about a year. Separately, an underwater survey found widespread coral bleaching—waters measured around 86°F, several degrees above optimal—with branching staghorn corals that dominated before 2023 wiped out by a severe marine heat wave; researchers noted recovery is possible only if waters cool and fishing pressures are removed.

No chart was warranted: the text provides no single unambiguous dataset suitable for one of the specified chart types, so visual is null.
items.title: Sea Shepherd Patrols Intercept Illegal Fishers Amid Coral Bleaching at Mexico's Scorpion Reef

items.summary: The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency's Clean Ports Program is directing $104 million toward zero-emission vehicles, equipment, and supporting infrastructure at four port sites across the state. Procurement has begun under a plan targeting Chicago's Illinois International Port District (IIPD), the Quad Cities, and southern Illinois river port districts. The funds are earmarked for heavy-duty electric assets including forklifts, reach stackers, switcher locomotives, charging infrastructure, and shore power systems for electrified ships, with one passenger ferry included among the equipment being modernized. Governor JB Pritzker, who was elected to a third term on November 3, stated that modernizing port infrastructure while advancing zero-emission technology would strengthen Illinois' economy and improve air quality. The program takes a holistic approach rather than simply swapping diesel for electric: at IIPD it integrates energy generation through on-site solar with storage for peak hours when grid electricity is most expensive, aiming to reduce strain on the local grid and hedge against rising energy costs; smaller public port districts receive support because replacing aging equipment and upgrading electrical infrastructure can be a large financial undertaking. The article includes promotional content from EnergySage recommending its solar installer service, which is unrelated to the program's funding or operations.
items.title: Illinois Clean Ports Program Allocates $104 Million for Zero-Emission Port Equipment

items.summary:
Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary and longtime ally of Donald Trump, is facing mounting bipartisan pressure amid a scandal involving his department's handling of advanced AI chip exports. The controversy centers on Megaspeed International, which was allegedly used as a conduit for diverting $4bn in Nvidia semiconductors to Chinese firms in breach of export controls—coinciding with the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, who is suspected by US intelligence agencies of being a Chinese spy. Lutnick's commerce department reportedly stalled enforcement efforts that other departments—the treasury, defense, and state—as well as the trade representative had pushed for months earlier.

The pressure has come from both parties. Republican Senator Tom Cotton told the Wall Street Journal that Lutnick repeatedly ignored warnings about AI chips being smuggled to China before the scandal became public, while Senators John Kennedy of Louisiana and Tim Scott of South Carolina have urged him to explain what he knew or testify before the Senate banking committee next month. Democrats Ron Wyden and Richard Neal wrote demanding that Lutnick preserve all records related to Nvidia chip export decisions, questioning whether political considerations improperly influenced policy, while Representatives Jamie Raskin, Gregory Meeks, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove launched an inquiry into whether Lutnick used his office to help Cantor Fitzgerald—now controlled by his sons—avoid losses connected to the Nvidia scrutiny.

Despite a vote of confidence from Trump on Friday—who described him as "a very good businessman" doing "a very good job"—critics are demanding his resignation, with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal calling for his departure and former Republican strategist Steve Schmidt asserting he should be fired. Adviser Kurt Bardella characterized Lutnick's outlook as a rough three to six months ahead once Democrats take control of Congress in January.

The article notes that these claims rest on allegations from intelligence agencies, senators, and officials rather than confirmed findings; the commerce department did not respond to comment requests.
items.title: Howard Lutnick Faces Congressional Investigations Over Nvidia Chip Sales to China

items.summary: For the second time this year, a record-setting AI company initial public offering paid Wall Street bankers more than half a billion dollars in fees while prompting private complaints about an unusually restrictive process. Anthropic's internal "Project Lantern" IPO eclipsed SpaceX's June deal and drew underwriters to more than $500 million in fees, but sources close to the transaction cited a compressed timeline with last-minute changes, delays sharing financial projections, rushed document approvals, and tight restrictions on bankers amid leak concerns. To limit information leaks after Reuters reported details from an S-1 draft nearly four weeks before its public filing, Anthropic instructed some of its 22 IPO underwriters to cap the number of participating bankers at four senior staff per firm — a restriction one source attributed to fear of leaks that banks reportedly worked around anyway; it also used NetRoadshow instead of standard PDFs so access logs and watermarks tracked who viewed documents. Separately, Anthropic asked some bank officers to sign legal agreements barring core transaction-team members from working with rival companies including OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek, and Hugging Face for six months after the listing — exclusivity that bankers described as rare on an individual level. These practices reflect a shifting power dynamic in which AI firms like SpaceX, Anthropic, and potentially OpenAI wield market demand to dictate terms their way; Jay Ritter of the University of Florida noted both companies negotiated zero spread on greenshoe over-allotment shares but suggested most issuers cannot expect that going forward. Both listings debuted successfully with oversubscribed order books, though post-listing share trajectories diverged: SpaceX peaked at $201.80 on June 16 before falling below its $135 IPO price in mid-July, while Anthropic's shares closed down 8.5 percent after a 17 percent first-day pop amid sector weakness. The reporting relies on people close to the process and declined-to-comment sources from Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic; figures are attributed as reported by Reuters without confirmation.
items.title: Anthropic's Record IPO Process Chafed Wall Street Bankers With Unusual Restrictions

items.summary:
Microsoft's Azure division is revising its compensation model to more tightly link employee performance with pay, according to a memo circulated by Arun Ulagaratchagan, executive vice-president of the Azure cloud computing division and reviewed by Bloomberg News. Under the changes reported by Bloomberg, top performers are set to receive larger stock awards while employees who fall short of expectations will be required to hold formal discussions with their managers. A Microsoft spokesperson stated that the revised system would provide substantial additional rewards for high-performing staff while ensuring workers have clear expectations and timely feedback from managers.

Ulagaratchagan framed the changes as a response to intensifying AI competition, writing that "pay-for-performance only works if we are equally rigorous on both sides: recognizing exceptional impact and being honest when performance falls short." He added that meeting current standards requires closing previous performance gaps and demonstrating meaningful improvement in results.

The article notes these measures reflect a broader industry trend toward higher performance expectations. It cites Elon Musk's 2022 ultimatum to Twitter employees demanding they commit to being "extremely hardcore" or leave with severance, and reports that an executive at Alphabet Inc.'s Google told division staff earlier this year that those not fully committed to AI could take voluntary buyout packages. Microsoft itself has cut tens of thousands of positions in recent years and is offering voluntary buyouts to roughly 60,000 employees.

The text does not provide specific details on the size of stock awards, the criteria for classifying performance as exceptional or below expectations, or how formal discussions will be conducted. All claims are attributed to Bloomberg reporting, Microsoft statements, or cited examples from other companies.
items.title: Microsoft Azure Ties Pay to Performance Amid AI Competition

items.summary: According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, the scandal involving Megaspeed—a Singapore-based company accused of supplying export-restricted Nvidia AI chips to China—has intensified scrutiny over its alleged smuggling network. While Alice Huang was publicly associated with the case due to her reported affair with former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and suspected links to Chinese intelligence, the report states she served only as the company's public face; behind the scenes, Chinese businessman Li Ming allegedly operated the smuggling operation. These disclosures emerge amid ongoing investigations by authorities in the US, Singapore, and Taiwan, alongside scrutiny of Jensen Huang's reported resignation from Nvidia and his relationship with Alice Huang. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and asserted that it complies with applicable export control regulations.
items.title: Chinese Businessman Allegedly Ran Nvidia Chip Smuggling Network Behind Public Face of Alice Huang

items.summary: Chris O'Shea, boss of British Gas owner Centrica, said he is 'hugely concerned' about the impact of an expected jump in household energy bills from January. He told the BBC that the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise as prices increase in the new year and described predictions of a substantial bill increase for Q1 as 'materially correct', noting that this is when most energy is consumed, coinciding with Christmas spending. The article reports these statements as O'Shea's views rather than established fact.
items.title: Centrica boss expresses concern over January energy bill increases

items.summary: Vahe Shahinian, a Glendale-based ticketing and concert-production entrepreneur who had built his business to roughly $5 million in annual sales with no missed payments, took what he believed was a preapproved line of credit from Wall Street–based EIN Cap. The broker pitched up to $750,000 at an annual rate just under 9%, conditioned on 30 days of daily $3,600 payments before the rest would be released; Shahinian received about $228,000 instead of a promised $250,000. When the line of credit never materialized after 30 days and continued to withhold funds through day 40, he says his bank account hit zero while tour expenses remained unpaid. He alleges fraud, describing it as bait-and-switch 'carroting'—dangling a low-interest loan offer to lure an unsolicited merchant cash advance (MCA). His lawsuit against EIN Cap is described by NPR as potentially the first of its kind to go to trial; his counsel for EIN declined comment and said only that MCA promises came from brokers, much of whose conduct remains in sealed depositions. Shahinian's account places his total accrued debt at roughly $5 million, including about $3 million in interest and fees, after he exhausted credit cards, home equity (his own, his parents', and a friend's), and eventually defaulted on debts to friends and family—among them Zorik Yeghikian, who had borrowed around $30,000 under similar MCA terms. His trial was delayed nine months before he lost his house to foreclosure at age 51 and moved in with his parents; several friends have urged him toward bankruptcy, which he rejects as admitting defeat. The article situates the case within a broader industry: MCAs are described by NPR as now the fastest-growing source of small-business funding in the U.S., largely unregulated because they are structured as purchases of future sales rather than loans, with fees ranging from 25% to over 200% on an annualized basis. Supporting figures cited include big banks rejecting about 20% of business loan applications and responding partially to a quarter per the Treasury Department; small-business bankruptcies rising alongside MCA use reported by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City; EIN's prior Illinois ruling ordering it to return $184,854 in profits from a firm accused of running a Ponzi-like scheme; and California legislation requiring funders and brokers to be licensed with background checks starting in 2028. The report notes Shahinian hired a private investigator to serve his lawsuit after tracking roughly 700 business owners sued by EIN, connected with about 70 who 'came to tears,' and that his counsel views the best-case outcome as a multimillion-dollar judgment with punitive damages while acknowledging uncertainty over what assets remain collectible. Limitations include NPR's reliance on Shahinian's account of events without independent verification, sealed depositions limiting disclosure of EIN-broker dealings, and no confirmed response from EIN about whether it still operates.
items.title: Ticketing Entrepreneur Sues MCA Funder Over Alleged Bait-and-Switch Loan That Triggered Seven Years of Debt

items.summary: A review by former minister Alan Milburn into young people not in employment, education or training (Neets) proposed that large employers give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 'meaningful feedback', as part of recommendations aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036. The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to their own systems. This addresses job ghosting, in which applicants receive no response after applying or interviewing; research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications were ignored. Yugraj Samrai, an unemployed graduate from Coventry, reported hearing nothing back about 30 to 40% of the time across hundreds of applications since July, while Ffion Johns, unemployed since June and interviewed only after 70 applications in September, cited a lack of feedback on why she was not selected. The Milburn report says this 'wall of silence' is especially damaging for young people because it offers nothing to learn from. Employers say they are flooded with applications in a competitive market, and artificial intelligence has added to the problem by enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications at once. Career coach Meg Burton suggested firms should at least inform unsuccessful applicants that AI could help achieve this, candidates should receive feedback if they reach an interview stage, and applicants can improve their chances by tailoring CVs rather than submitting many identical applications while never taking ghosting personally.
items.title: UK Review Proposes Feedback for Unsuccessful Young Applicants Amid Rise in Job Ghosting

items.summary: In a piece titled "Li Dongsheng: Think Globally, Build Locally," the publication traveled to Shenzhen to examine whether innovation can bring the Asia-Pacific region closer together. The article profiles Li Dongsheng, founder and chairman of TCL, who has witnessed China's entire reform-and-opening-up period. According to the text, he opened his first overseas factory in Vietnam in 1999, nearly failed after his initial major overseas deals, and subsequently recovered. He now frames his approach as "Globalization 3.0," defined by taking domestic strengths abroad while ensuring local economies grow alongside him.
items.title: TCL Founder Li Dongsheng Describes 'Globalization 3.0' Strategy

items.summary: A CGTN documentary titled 'From fishing to farming: The journey of China's seafood industry' examines how China shifted from harvesting wild fish to cultivating farmed seafood. According to figures cited in the text, by the late 1990s China had become the world's largest producer and consumer of food fish, and its aquaculture output now exceeds its wild catch. The program begins in Xiamen as it investigates how this transition occurred and considers what measures might protect marine ecosystems amid expanding production. It is important to note that these statistics are presented within a promotional description rather than verified independently; the text functions primarily as an introduction or teaser for the documentary, offering context about its subject matter without providing detailed evidence or analysis of the claims it makes.
items.title: CGTN Documentary Explores the Transformation of China's Seafood Industry

items.summary: Negotiators at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) concluded a late-night closing plenary around midnight on Friday, November 21, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, with the final outcome document anticipated to be released over the weekend. COP31 President Murat Kurum stated that "very little distance remains" and urged delegations to prioritize consensus over individual priorities, expressing hope for an "Antalya Consensus." Negotiations Chair Chris Bowen added on Friday that parties would continue working "for as long as it takes," citing a "spirit of goodwill" among delegations. The latest draft texts centered on climate finance, adaptation support, clean energy, electrification, and carbon capture. COP31 opened November 9 with representatives from nearly 200 parties focused on delivering on climate pledges.
items.title: COP31 closing session ends in Antalya with outcome document expected over the weekend

items.summary: Tristan Sharratt, a family nurse practitioner and public health researcher at Binghamton University who serves an Amish community of several hundred people in central New York, argues that 'trusted messengers'—individuals such as neighbors, midwives, or long-distance drivers who have earned respect within Plain Anabaptist communities—are essential to addressing the ongoing measles outbreak. Sharratt stated that trust-building with these communities requires months to years and cannot be achieved by simply announcing an outbreak and urging vaccination; instead, outreach should center on human connection, building peer relationships first before discussing health issues. The current outbreak has killed at least eight people across Pennsylvania (eight), Wisconsin (two), New York (one), and Virginia (one). Sharratt attributed the vaccine hesitancy in these communities partly to their belief in Gelassenheit ('God's will') and 'plain living,' while noting that anti-vaccine activism accelerated during the pandemic, with non-Amish groups such as Children's Health Defense—then led by Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—targeting Plain Anabaptist publications with vaccine misinformation. He cited informal community connections, including local business owners or contractors who spend extended time near Amish families, and pointed to the Otsego County health department for successfully maintaining relationships with two Amish communities since a pertussis outbreak roughly two decades ago through recurring vaccine clinics. Sharratt identified significant limitations: public health agencies often lack accurate data on Plain Anabaptist populations—including population size, number of children, and vaccination rates—requiring a return to older community-based epidemiological methods; healthcare access remains difficult because most Amish rely on shared community insurance while providers typically accept conventional coverage or charge cost-prohibitive fees as medicine becomes more profit-driven; and each Amish community must be treated as a unique entity with its own decisions, including variability in how individual families respond to anti-vaccine perspectives. Sharratt expressed optimism that trust, once established through sustained community engagement, can spread rapidly alongside infectious disease.
items.title: Public Health Experts Point to Trusted Messengers as Key Strategy Amid Amish Measles Outbreak

items.summary: Guardian Australia analysis of Hansard records from 2006 to 2026 found that profanity and language deemed unparliamentary rose significantly, with 2026 recorded as the worst year on record. The number of swear words increased by 78% since 2006, reaching approximately 37 profane instances per million words spoken in parliament this year. Language considered unparliamentary must be withdrawn or MPs face ejection from the chamber, though politicians have continued to use such language at a record rate. Speaker Milton Dick said he believes debate has actually improved during his tenure since 2022, attributing part of that perception to increased volume rather than tone. The analysis found most swearing comes from the Senate, which saw a 177% increase in bad language since 2006; among active participants (those speaking at least 100,000 words), Bill Heffernan was the lead offender with an expletive use-rate of 877 per million words spoken between 2006 and 2016. Jacqui Lambie ranked second, responsible for 6% of total swearing at a rate of 406 per million words. When excluding quotes, idioms and literal uses, own-use swearing nearly tripled from 6.4 per million words in 2006-9 to 18.9 in 2022-5. Broken down by party, One Nation swore at 7.4 times the rate of Labor. The analysis categorized language into mild (such as bloody and damn), strong (prick, shit) and extreme terms (fucking, cunt). Swearing numbers were converted to a per-million-word rate to control for tenure length and verbosity, and an LLM was used with 97% manual agreement on whether uses were the speaker's own voice. The figures are approximate due to this methodology.
items.title: Australian Parliament Sets New Swearing Record in 2026

items.summary: On Sunday, November 22 in Manchester, reigning Women's Super League champions Manchester City failed to move into first place after a 3-1 home defeat by Tottenham Hotspur. The result left City second in the standings on 25 points from 11 games, two behind leaders Chelsea and two ahead of third-placed London City Lionesses. City had taken a 1-0 lead through Bunny Shaw's goal in the 10th minute while leaders Chelsea were held to a 1-1 draw by Liverpool on Saturday; however, Tottenham equalized just before halftime when Cathinka Tandberg leveled for Norway. Spurs then took control after Drew Spence sliced open City with a pass through the middle in the 74th minute and Matilda Vinberg put it into the net, with Jessica Naz adding her goal on her 100th WSL appearance to make it 3-1. The loss lifted Tottenham to fifth place on 20 points. In another early kick-off that day, Simi Awujo scored deep into second-half stoppage time to give Manchester United a 2-1 away win over Birmingham City, leaving them fourth in the table on 21 points.
items.title: Manchester City miss chance for WSL top spot with shock loss to Tottenham

items.summary: FRANCE 24 published a photo recap titled 'The week in pictures,' reviewing notable events from the past week. The central event was an unprecedented summit held in Shenzhen, China, where President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Alongside this diplomatic gathering, the recap highlighted tough negotiations at COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, as well as another week of French protests driven by cost-of-living concerns. The text presents these items as a retrospective collection of striking images rather than offering analysis or verification of their underlying claims.
items.title: FRANCE 24 Reviews Key Events From a Week Featuring Xi's Shenzhen Summit and COP31

items.summary: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey failed to reach a consensus on its final agreement after the European Union and several other countries rejected a draft proposal that omitted any mention of fossil fuels. COP31 President Murat Kurum acknowledged at the conference's closing session that no agreement existed because these decisions had not been adopted. The dispute centered on fossil fuels as the key driver of climate change; Ireland's EU presidency minister Darragh O'Brien stated the bloc would refuse to endorse a deal lacking mention of fossil fuels, adding that the draft did not meet current needs. Negotiations unfolded amid an evolving text: after one version called for accelerated phasing out of these energy sources, a subsequent Thursday release removed all references entirely, prompting France and Panama to issue a letter demanding a clear transition away from fossil fuels. UN Secretary General António Guterres expressed deep disappointment in a statement emphasizing that those profiting from environmental destruction should not dictate climate policy terms. Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen also voiced his frustration over the failed cover decision. The summit became the longest-ever UN climate conference, with negotiations extending two days beyond their scheduled conclusion.
items.title: COP31 Climate Talks Collapse After EU Rejects Fossil Fuel Omission

items.summary: Rescue and firefighting efforts continued for the Russian cargo vessel Sparta II, which was hit by a drone strike before drifting into Finnish waters. The ship was bound for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad when it was struck Saturday morning around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT), approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the eastern Gulf of Finland, according to Finland's Border Guard. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack; Kyiv had not yet commented as of Sunday. Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh stated that two drones were used based on preliminary information and reported no threat to supplies there. Firefighting with water continued into Sunday, with Finland noting Estonian and Russian assets also participated in recovery work. The Border Guard said it was working to prevent the ship from sinking but detected no environmental damage and assessed no danger to surrounding maritime traffic or people. Crew members were evacuated onto another Russian vessel that had departed for Russia, while a separate Russian rescue vessel remained at the stricken ship's location; earlier reports suggested the crew declined evacuation before being moved. The Sparta II was sanctioned by both the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year and is operated by a company it said was established within Russia's defence ministry structure in 2011 and has run as part of the military construction complex since 2015, per Ukrainian and US governments. The incident prompted temporary aviation and maritime restrictions around the area, and Finland's defence ministry reported that a Russian helicopter may have violated Finnish airspace shortly after, potentially linked to rescue or tracking operations; NATO was also informed. Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said the Border Guard led the investigation in cooperation with other authorities. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo characterized the event as war spilling into Russia's immediate vicinity and affirmed Ukraine's right to respond against what he called an aggressor.
items.title: Russia-bound cargo ship Sparta II remains on fire after suspected Ukrainian drone attack in eastern Gulf of Finland

items.summary: World leaders departed the UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, without a new agreement after debate broke down over a draft that failed to explicitly mention fossil fuels. The joint proposal from COP31 presidents Australia and Türkiye was rejected on Sunday afternoon local time by several countries and the 27-nation European Union following two weeks of negotiations and double overtime — making it the longest UN climate summit ever, at roughly 44 hours past the official close. Ireland's EU-rotating presidency climate minister Darragh O'Brien refused to endorse what he called a 'cover decision' that did not name fossil fuels, describing the talks as 'hijacked by some oil states,' while Russia and Saudi Arabia supported leaving them out. Australian energy minister Chris Bowen called the outcome 'very disappointing' but said Australia left nothing on the table; several other nations accepted consensus reluctantly. The draft instead referenced a 2023 global deal that shifts away from fossil fuels without naming them explicitly, though that 2023 agreement remains one of only two such deals in the past 25 years to name fossil fuels directly. The failed text included Türkiye's goal of raising electricity's share of total final world energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 from around 23 per cent, a carbon-capture-and-storage technology target backed by the oil industry, and an unspecified tripling of climate finance for developing countries rather than stating a baseline. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres expressed 'profound frustration' with governments he said failed to rise to the moment, following October's confirmation that global temperature rises will exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold set at Paris over a decade ago. The article notes as a limitation that this failure does not erase obligations from previous conferences or remove existing technical and legal frameworks for multilateral climate action; it also states that the last time UN talks failed to adopt a deal was in Copenhagen in 2009.
items.title: COP31 Climate Summit Ends Without Deal After Draft Omits Fossil Fuels

items.summary: Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara announced that Japan's government intends to convene a council on reducing the burden of the U.S. Marine Corps' Futenma air base in Okinawa by year-end at the earliest, responding to a request from Okinawa Governor Genta Koja during a meeting in Naha. The council for promoting alleviation of burdens from the Futenma base had not met since April 2019. Kihara's remarks marked his first visit to Okinawa since Koja took office in September, and he expressed intentions to cooperate with the prefectural government on local economic development. During the same trip, Kihara attended a ceremony marking the completion of restoration work on Shuri Castle's main hall after its 2019 fire damage, visited a park developed on a U.S. military housing site slated for return to Japan, and toured University of the Ryukyus Hospital.
items.title: Japan Plans Futenma Burden-Reduction Council Meeting by Year-End

items.summary: At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye's Environment Minister and COP31 president Murat Kurum said on Sunday that some countries obstructed progress by fixating on wording and introducing issues unrelated to climate change. Speaking after a plenary session, he stated the presidency had proposed measures to expand renewable energy, protect oceans and mountains, uphold the Paris Agreement's 1.5C temperature goal, and promote carbon capture technologies aligned with the agreement; however, some countries supported the proposed cover decision while others opposed it, preventing consensus. Kurum said Türkiye would not prepare another draft in the absence of consensus, warning that continued deadlock would only worsen climate change impacts and criticizing a system built around meetings without decisions. He credited Türkiye and Australia for facilitating compromise throughout the summit and noted the final responsibility for reaching consensus rests with all 196 participating countries.
items.title: COP31 President Blames Unrelated Issues and Word Fixation for Blocked Climate Progress

items.summary: On Sunday, Japan's Justice Ministry announced that Toshiaki Masunaga, an 78-year-old death-row inmate convicted in connection with a series of corporate bombings mainly in Tokyo during the 1970s, died at the Tokyo Detention House. The ministry stated he had been undergoing treatment for a cerebral infarction but did not disclose the cause of death. Masunaga was a member of the East Asia Anti-Japan Armed Front, and his death coincided with the announcement that Japan's total number of inmates holding finalized death sentences now stands at 99. According to the final ruling dated Aug. 30, 1974, Masunaga conspired with former death-row inmate Masashi Daidoji—who died in 2017—and others to plant and detonate a time bomb outside a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries building in Tokyo's Marunouchi district; eight people were killed in that bombing. Between 1971 and 1975, Masunaga was involved in a total of 14 bombing incidents, including an attempted bombing of a special train carrying the Emperor. At his trial at Tokyo District Court in 1979, he and Daidoji were sentenced to death on grounds that the crime was unprecedented in its cruelty, viciousness, and vileness; the sentence was upheld by the Tokyo High Court, and the Supreme Court rejected Masunaga's final appeal in 1987. Of nine people arrested over the bombings, eight were indicted (one had committed suicide), with two death sentences finalized alongside one life-imprisonment term and three fixed-term prison terms. Separately, suspects Norio Sasaki and Ayako Daidoji remain on international wanted lists after being released under an extraordinary measure following the 1975 seizure of the U.S. Embassy in Kuala Lumpur by the Japanese Red Army; and Satoshi Kirishima, a group member who was questioned by Tokyo police in 2024 while hiding in Kanagawa Prefecture, later died at a hospital before prosecutors declined to indict him.
items.title: Japan's Justice Ministry reports death of Toshiaki Masunaga, a 1970s corporate-bombing death-row inmate

items.summary: A fire broke out at an Indonesian factory that produces sweets and snack products, killing at least three people and leaving 36 individuals unaccounted for. Fifteen survivors were rescued from the plant while firefighters continued battling flames across multiple sections of the facility more than 12 hours after the blaze began. The cause remains unknown, though a survivor reported it originated in a cooling unit on the third floor.
items.title: Fire at Indonesian sweets factory leaves three dead and dozens missing

items.summary: Agathon Rwasa, ousted from the National Congress for Freedom party (CNDD-FDD) in March 2024 during an extraordinary congress held under heavy police protection by dissident MPs who accused him of rule violations and fracturing the movement, has applied to stand as an independent candidate in Burundi's next presidential election. He faces a conflict between an electoral commission provision requiring party officials to resign before running independently and his reading of the Constitution, which he says is unambiguous: it permits candidacy two years after removal from office but not resignation. Rwasa characterized his ouster as a government attempt to exclude him from the poll and claimed continued support by citing the party's second-place finish in 2010 elections—though he acknowledged opposition claims that vote was marred by fraud—and reported raising 100 million (currency unspecified) for his deposit, arguing individual citizens rather than parties determine outcomes. Meanwhile, outgoing president Évariste Ndayishimiye and ruling-party candidate submitted the first application to the electoral commission ahead of a first-round poll scheduled for 3 May 2027, with a possible runoff on 1 June; no election outcome or final candidacy approvals are reported here.
items.title: Ex-opposition leader Agathon Rwasa to run as independent in Burundi's 2027 presidential poll

items.summary: A major fire at the Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Serang Regency, Banten province, western Java, left at least six body bags recovered by a joint emergency team. Indonesian police reported that the blaze began around 4:30 pm on Saturday and was extinguished by 6:30 am on Sunday. Of the 54 recorded employees, 11 returned home while one is receiving medical treatment; the remaining 42 are unaccounted for as crews continue to coordinate with families and the company to verify their whereabouts.
items.title: At Least Six Recovered After Candy Factory Fire in Banten, Western Java

items.summary:
The Lowy Institute's 2026 Asia Power Index found that the United States lost significant power and influence across Asia while China gained ground, with the gap between the two superpowers' military capabilities reaching its narrowest point on record. According to data analyst Jack Sato, this narrowing reflects a decline in US power rather than an advance by Beijing; authors Hunter Marston and Jack Sato attributed it primarily to Washington's missteps—specifically the Trump administration's diversion of resources from the Pacific to the Middle East over what the report describes as its "unresolved war with Iran," which depleted long-range missile stockpiles, plus pressure on allies to fund their own defence and reduce joint exercises. The US-China economic capability gap narrowed to 5.3 points, still a clear lead for Washington but the closest since the index's inception; China ranked first in both Economic Relationship and Diplomatic Influence measures ahead of the US. Survey respondents viewed the United States as distracted and disengaged from Asia.

South-East Asian nations faced mounting pressure amid Middle East conflict disruptions to global energy supplies, higher fuel and fertiliser prices constraining food production, South China Sea tensions, and competition between the two powers; government effectiveness declined across nearly all countries except Singapore, Myanmar and Laos, while diplomatic influence fell in almost every nation. Indonesia recorded the largest drop in diplomatic influence, attributed largely to what the report calls a "haphazard approach to foreign policy" under President Prabowo Subianto.

India emerged as more influential overall despite most regional states declining diplomatically; Prime Minister Narendra Modi is now rated the second-most effective regional leader behind Xi Jinping. Sato credited continuity between Modi and External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, noting India's political influence has grown since the index began eight years ago—though China's power remains 80 per cent higher than India's—and that India's Economic Capability and Resilience scores decreased amid internal challenges while its Diplomatic Influence dipped only slightly.

Australia's comprehensive power score fell slightly to sixth place, behind Russia; Sato credited Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with advancing economic interests but rated him less effective on diplomatic goals. The report presents these findings as survey-based assessments of regional perceptions and capabilities rather than absolute measurements.
items.title: Lowy Institute's 2026 Asia Power Index Finds US-China Gap at Record Narrow as Washington Loses Regional Influence

items.summary: Around 4,000 Palestinian refugees living in Geziret Fadel village in Sharqiya province, northern Egypt, exist in a state of legal limbo as foreigners despite most having been born in the country. Their families fled historic Palestine during the 1948 Arab-Israeli war that ended with the establishment of Israel and concluded in March 1949; residents describe this displacement as the Nakba. Ninety-year-old Shamma Abu Hussein, who escaped from Beersheba (now in southern Israel), is described as possibly the last person in Egypt to have lived in historic Palestine, having watched three generations grow up while losing her mother during the flight. The community faces concrete barriers accessing education, healthcare, and other public services because they are treated as foreigners even though many were born in Egypt. Selmi Soliman al-Namouli, a 63-year-old agricultural labourer with ten children who was himself born in Egypt, reported that residency renewals paid for in US dollars, school fees, and other administrative costs burden his family enough to prevent him from sending his daughter Asmaa to university; his nephew Farid Khaled al-Namouli left school over paperwork obstacles and took work at a village clothing shop. According to the Palestinian refugee rights organisation BADIL, researchers estimate around 50,000 Palestinians displaced by earlier conflicts were living in Egypt before the Gaza war began, with more than 100,000 additional arrivals since that conflict started. Egyptian officials state they provide medical care and education to Palestinian refugees and oppose permanent displacement from their land; under former president Gamal Abdel Nasser these residents once enjoyed access to education and employment largely on par with Egyptian citizens. After Egypt's 1978 peace treaty with Israel and the assassination of culture minister Yusuf Sibai by the Abu Nidal group, regulations were tightened. UNWRA counts 3.5 million registered Palestinians in Jordan, Syria and Lebanon but has never operated in Egypt; Oxford emeritus professor Dawn Chatty noted that education enabled refugees elsewhere to find work abroad through remittances, which did not occur for those in Egypt. Successive Egyptian governments have rejected naturalising Palestinians on the grounds it could undermine their right of return.
items.title: Palestinian refugees born in Egypt live without legal status or access to services

items.summary: A super El Niño developing in the Pacific is projected to strengthen toward the end of 2026 and persist into early 2027, with scientists warning it will amplify dangerous heat across parts of Africa. The event unfolds within a climate system already warmed by decades of greenhouse gas emissions, so its effects vary regionally rather than uniformly; danger arises not from temperature alone but from combined heat stress driven by temperature, humidity, wind, and sunlight that impairs the body's ability to cool itself. A hydroclimate and health scientist who studied African heat exposure reports that a multi-model ensemble of bias-corrected climate projections found more than 60% of urban populations in west and central Africa could face strong or extreme heat stress by century's end. The same researcher's continent-wide study covering 1974 to 2023 found very strong and extreme heat stress became more frequent, persistent, and widespread, with three-to-five-day and six-to-eight-day episodes doubling in some locations while several hours of daily strain occurred across many countries; the proportion of hottest-season hours under such conditions rose by 2 to 25 percentage points over that span. The researcher cautions these historical findings do not directly predict death tolls for this specific El Niño event, and notes weak health surveillance can leave cases uncounted while attributing deaths to underlying illnesses. Recommended preparations include joint meteorological-health warnings, hospital heat-response plans with backup power and ventilation, adjusted school and outdoor work hours, improved recording of heat-related illness and death, and funding triggered by climate warnings before conditions become catastrophic.
items.title: Developing super El Niño expected to intensify Africa's heat crisis by late 2026

items.summary: Following an International Court of Justice ruling on Thursday that held Myanmar responsible for genocide against Rohingya Muslims during its 2017 military operations in northern Rakhine State, Malaysia announced it would engage the UN, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and ASEAN to pursue a lasting solution. The ICJ judgment ordered Myanmar to provide reparations to victims and take measures to prevent further violations; the case was brought by The Gambia in 2019. In its statement, Malaysia's Foreign Ministry said it respects the ruling as consistent with its position on protecting vulnerable communities and would advocate for a comprehensive resolution while engaging parties to implement concrete protective measures for Rohingya sheltered within Malaysian territory.
items.title: Malaysia Pledges Regional Engagement After ICJ Genocide Ruling Against Myanmar

items.summary: Colombia is described as a nation where nearly eight out of 10 people believe miracles occur, with the figure rising to over nine out of 10 among evangelical Christians according to a National University survey. This belief underpins the political prominence of evangelicals, exemplified by President Abelardo de la Espriella's campaign slogan "The Homeland of Miracles." Despite this cultural influence, Pew Research Center data shows only about 20% of Colombian adults identified as evangelicals in 2019, with a more recent survey placing evangelicals and other Protestants at just 15% of the adult population—lower than Brazil's 29% and Chile's 19%, yet still politically significant. Catholics remain the largest religious group at 60% of adults, though they are losing members: among those raised Catholic who left the faith, eight out of every 100 have moved to Protestant churches while 13 report having no religion. Evangelicals gained political power under Álvaro Uribe (president 2002-2010) and later Iván Duque, with figures like Pastor Marco Fidel Acosta heading the National Savings Fund and John Milton Rodríguez tasked with dismantling the Ministry of Equality. The movement's influence is tied to prosperity theology—where tithing promises financial return—and a moral agenda opposing rights that Colombia had previously established: euthanasia decriminalization in 1997, same-sex marriage legalization in 2016, and abortion up to the 24th week permitted since 2022. A key political turning point occurred when Paloma Valencia won Uribe's party primary but lost evangelical support after choosing openly gay Juan Daniel Oviedo as running mate; congressman Daniel Briceño attributes this loss partly to legislation he promoted that churches viewed as promoting "gender ideology" in schools, triggering a domino effect of conservative Catholic defections. Pew Research Center data from 2024 indicates Colombia is the Latin American country most wanting Bible influence on laws: 69% support it compared to 66% in Brazil and Peru.
items.title: Rising Evangelical Influence in Colombia's Politics and Society

items.summary: As the Republican Party lost control in the midterm elections, Donald Trump's presidency entered its final phase amid diminished congressional support and a contested 2028 succession battle. With opposition to the war in Iran gaining momentum and Venezuela receding as an issue, Cuba remained Washington's primary lever—reinforced by the reelection of three Cuban American members of Congress from Florida, though voter fatigue was emerging. Since military operations in Caracas, Maduro's arrest, and a tightened oil embargo on Cuba, the Trump administration pursued a dual strategy combining threats of full-scale invasion or targeted strikes with an escalating sanctions regime aimed at weakening Havana's ruling elite; however, recent crackdowns on journalists and activists suggest that power remained intact despite deteriorating living conditions. The analysis holds that Washington's punitive logic targets either internal collapse or negotiations, but an invasion would eliminate both possibilities simultaneously—making negotiation the only viable outcome absent external military action or internal rebellion, especially given Cuba's unprecedented structural dependence on the United States. Cuban proposals for limited economic opening without political reform were rejected by Trump and State Department Secretary Marco Rubio, who may be seeking arrangements perceived as 'regime change.' Any resumed negotiations would face three entrenched constituencies: a confrontational wing of the Cuban American community (weakening with declining Trumpism), hard-line factions within Cuba, and Havana's ideological international support network. Although these opposition forces are weaker than ever—China, Russia, Brazil, and Mexico not challenging Washington—their capacity to derail talks and preserve the status quo remains intact, potentially prolonging sanctions-driven poverty, inequality, shortages, and repression for Cuba's low-income majority.
items.title: Cuba at the End of Trump: U.S. Strategy Shifts Toward Invasion Threats and Sanctions

items.summary: A New York Times report describes a Chinese intelligence campaign that predates recent allegations involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and businesswoman Alice Huang, framing it as part of Beijing's broader effort to circumvent Western export restrictions. According to the report—which cites serving and former security officials from Asia, the United States, and Europe—China's spy agency created a dedicated working group under its director, Chen Yixin, tasked with helping Chinese companies acquire and smuggle advanced chips while gathering intelligence on semiconductor supply chains. The unit reports directly to Chen, who announced the expanded mission in April amid calls to overcome technology blockades; President Xi Jinping had separately urged officials in January to take extraordinary measures against bottlenecks in critical sectors. Separately, the Trump administration introduced a rule requiring overseas data centers to obtain government licenses before supplying substantial computing capacity to companies headquartered in countries including China, Russia, and Iran, with enforcement set for roughly 90 days. The report notes that China has dismissed the espionage allegations as "pure fabrication," while Alice Huang declined comment requests.
items.title: New York Times Reports China Established Dedicated Spy Unit to Acquire Advanced Chips

items.summary: Machine learning researcher and former software engineer at Google and Microsoft, Nate Soares, told The Atlantic's CEO Nicholas Thompson on a recent podcast that he believes there is greater than a 50% chance artificial intelligence will cause human extinction within the next 10 years. His forecast comes roughly two months after three Anthropic researchers warned of similar risks; Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in protest over what he claimed were mishandled responses to AI's threat, and had previously worked at OpenAI. Soares said his conviction is strong enough that he stopped contributing to his 401K about a decade ago, though he retains an existing account from his time at Google. He serves as president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, a Berkeley-based nonprofit associated with 'AI doomerism,' and does not view extinction as inevitable; instead, he said he spends his efforts trying to prevent it while otherwise living normally, comparing the experience to coping with historical threats like plague and war. When Thompson pushed back by noting that even advanced AI systems still encounter limitations, Soares dismissed this reassurance, likening current AI capabilities to early automobiles—arguing that critics once pointed out what cars could not yet do as models improved over time. He also stated he is not concerned about mass unemployment from AI, saying humanity would reach full employment 'the moment before we're all killed off.' The article's framing of Soares' views relies on his own testimony and the reported claims of Anthropic researchers; Thompson directly challenged the extinction scenario by citing existing AI limitations.
items.title: Former Google AI engineer Nate Soares says humans may have fewer than 10 years left

items.summary:
According to a Wall Street Journal report citing people familiar with the matter and corporate registry records, 52-year-old Li Ming—a Chinese national identified as Century Longteng's chief strategy officer—was central to operations at Singapore-based Megaspeed and had connections to other companies trading Nvidia chips. In February 2025, Singapore prosecutors charged Li and others with fraud over alleged transshipment of Nvidia-equipped servers; while several firms were named in the case, Megaspeed was not among them. Prosecutors allege Li misrepresented equipment destined for his company Luxuriate Your Life, shipped it to Malaysia, then forwarded it onward.

Li worked with Alice Huang and her husband Kang Wei, who established Century Longteng cloud-computing joint venture in 2021. The trio built a Southeast Asian network providing computing capacity to Chinese customers by acquiring the Singapore unit of a Chinese video game company and renaming it Megaspeed, where Huang was registered as director. After telling Nvidia that Alibaba was an anchor customer, Megaspeed joined its cloud partner programme in November 2023, gaining priority access to processors; prosecutors allege some servers were sent to Shanghai-based Century Litong—controlled by Century Longteng until 2024—in violation of US export controls.

Nvidia placed Megaspeed on an internal 'no sell' list in June 2025 amid investigations. Singapore questioned Huang over chip-smuggling suspicions, allowed her departure, and barred re-entry; she left the company in August 2025, which Megaspeed said went dormant afterward.

The team reportedly launched Novagate Cloud in 2025, an Nvidia cloud partner operating at least two data centres with Blackwell chips. WSJ-reviewed shipment records show a Malaysian entity received over $300 million worth of Nvidia-chip hardware during the first five months of 2026, and corporate links tie Novagate to Century Litong-associated companies; its directors also hold positions in firms connected to another individual charged with similar offences.

The report relies on sources described as 'people familiar with' the matter rather than direct confirmation. Li remains out on bail while the criminal case continues.
items.title: Singapore Fraud Charges Link Chinese National to Nvidia Chip-Smuggling Network Tied to Alice Huang

items.summary: On November 21, a costume contest called the 'Chinese Spy Lookalike Contest' was held at Washington Square Park in New York. Organized by FactMachine and Prez, the event featured participants dressing as spy-inspired characters—some reportedly miming retrieving classified documents while another impersonated Jensen Huang—and performing mock spy acts for spectators. Audience members voted via QR codes to determine a winner who received a $50 (approximately ₹4,636) cash prize. Videos of the gathering circulated on social media after the event. The contest drew its theme from an unresolved espionage controversy involving Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspected of gathering information for Beijing; China has rejected these claims as not conclusively established. The matter also raised questions about her reported relationship with Jensen Huang and concerns over possible transfers of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, reflecting broader US-China tensions around artificial intelligence technology and semiconductor exports. Separately, Jensen Huang reportedly acknowledged an affair and apologized to his family and employees while Nvidia's board initiated an independent investigation into the matter.
items.title: New York 'Chinese Spy Lookalike Contest' Held at Washington Square Park on November 21

items.summary: In its World Energy Outlook 2026, the International Energy Agency (IEA) projects that India will install an additional 200 million air conditioners in homes over the next decade, making it the biggest driver of global energy demand growth. Under the agency's Stated Policies Scenario, India and Southeast Asia's share of the global AC stock would rise from less than 10 percent today to 20 percent by 2035; currently fewer than one in five households own an AC despite high cooling needs, compared with around 90 percent ownership in Australia, Japan, and the United States. The IEA noted that for the first time in energy history, building demand for cooling is overtaking demand for heating. India's electricity demand would grow about 6 percent annually over the next decade—the fastest of any major region—while total energy demand rises roughly 2.5 percent per year, triple the global rate. Globally, space-cooling demand could rise by 1,700 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2035, an increase described as roughly equivalent to India's total electricity demand today; in a modeled heatwave case, cooling demand growth would be about 40 percent higher at around 700 TWh. Under the Current Policies Scenario, global peak cooling demand is expected to grow by 720 gigawatts by 2035—more than India's entire generation capacity today—and faster adoption of more efficient appliances could reduce India's seasonal power-demand swings despite similar electrification levels. The report also cited weather effects: an early and strong 2025 monsoon depressed electricity demand and boosted hydropower, helping keep coal demand in check for the world's second-biggest coal consumer. Beyond cooling, the IEA expects India to add over 12,000 cars a day, see a 33 percent rise in built space, surge steel and cement production, and raise energy investment by roughly 85 percent by 2035 from 2025 levels—the fastest-growing major destination for such spending. India generated about 2,114 TWh of electricity in 2025, projected to rise to 3,585 TWh by 2035 with 51 percent from non-fossil sources; coal remains a mainstay and the agency projects CO2 emissions do not peak until around 2040. These figures are projections under specific IEA scenarios (Stated Policies Scenario and Current Policies Scenario) rather than observed data, and weather variability could alter actual outcomes.
items.title: IEA Projects India to Add 200 Million Household Air Conditioners by 2035, Becoming the Largest Driver of Global Energy Demand Growth

items.summary: RailTel Corporation of India Ltd, a Mumbai-based Navratna public sector undertaking, received an order worth approximately ₹27.03 crore (₹27,02,56,350 including taxes) from Andhra Pradesh Technology Services to develop and operate a statewide AI-powered legal assistant platform for the Andhra Pradesh government on Google Cloud Platform. The company notified stock exchanges of the Letter of Acceptance on November 22, with the work order itself received on November 21 at 5:29 pm. RailTel stated it will handle design, development, implementation, hosting, and managed services across multiple stages, including deployment and ongoing infrastructure management. The contract is classified as a domestic order awarded by Andhra Pradesh Technology Services, and RailTel has until May 9, 2029, to execute the project, indicating a multi-year arrangement. Under Regulation 30 of SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2015, RailTel disclosed that neither its promoters nor promoter group entities hold any interest in the awarding body and that the transaction is not a related-party deal.
